THE TIDES.
By the action of the sun and moon, especially the latter, the waters of
the large oceans of the earth are drawn in the directions of these bodies,
| so as to'rise and fall according to their position in relation to them.
These regular movements are called THe TspEs.
The movement of the waters in the tides chiefly follows the course of
the moon. The lunar day, or interval from the moon being on the
| meridian of any place, till she is again on that meridian, is 24 hours 50
minutes, in consequence of the rapid motion of the moon through the
| sky. Hence the phenomena of the tides take place in this period.
There are two Hicgu-WATERsS or F': sops at the same time, one on the
meridian next the moon, the other :« the opposite meridian; and at
every place there are two high-tides in the lunar day, at an interval of
about 12 hours 25 minutes. The tides are the highest when the sun and
moon are in conjunction or opposition—then called spring-tides ; lowest
when the moon is in her quarters—then called neap-tides. The tides are
| affected by the moon’s distance, the sun’s distance and elevation, and
[| by local causes.
The tide on the side of the earth next the moon is caused by the direct
| action of the moon, in drawing towards her the waters there. But the
moon also acts on the mass of the earth, as well as the waters under her ;
| hence she, in a manner, gives the earth a tendency from the water on the
| farther side of the earth, which produces a high tide on that side also.

& small, long-haired furniture-brush; after which wipe it closely with clean flan-
nels, and rub it with dry bread.
lf properly done, the curtains will look nearly as well as at first; and if the

Pold in large parcels, and put carefully by. |
While the furniture remains up, it should be preserved from the sun and air as |
much as possible, which injure delicate colours; and the dust may be blown off’
with bellows.

To wa! : Hens Lay Perperuatty.—Hene will lay perpetually if treated in the
f-llowing manner :—Keep no rouvstera (cocks): give the hens fresh meat, chopped
up like sxusage meat, once a day ; a very small portion, say half an ounce a day to
‘each hen, during the winter, or from the time insects disappear in the fall till
_ they appear again in the spring. Never allow an egg to remain in the nest for
| what are called “nest eggs.’ When the roosters do not run with the hens, and no
| nest eggs are left in the nest, the hens will not cease laying after the production of
twelve or fifteen eggs, as they always do when roosters and nest eggs are alluwed ;
, but continue lv ying perpetually. The only reason wry hens do not lay in winter
| a8 freely as in summer, is the want of animal food, which they get in summer in
| abundance, in the form of insects.

Maxrtna Beps.—Close or press bedsteads are il] adapted for young persons or |
invalids; when their use is unavoidable, the bed-clothes should be displaced every |
morning, and left for a short time before they are shut up. The windows of bed- |
rooms should be kept open for some hours every day, to carry off the effluvia from |
the bed-clothes; the bed should also be shaken up, and the clothes spread about, |
in which state the longer they remain, the better. The bed being made, the |
clothes should not be tucked in at the sides or foot, as that prevents any further |
purification taking place, by the cool air passing through them,
A warming pan should be chosen with holes in the lid. About a yard of moder” |
ately-sized iron chain, made red-hot and put into the pan, is a simple and excellent |
substitute for coals.

EXCELLENT Metnop or Reartne Catves.—Put some water on the fire, nearly
the quantity that the calf can drink. When it boils, throw into it one or two
handsful of oatmeal, and suffer the whole to !:oil for a minute. Then suffer it to
cool until new-milk-warm. Then mix with it one or two quarts of milk that has
stood twelve hours, and has been skimmed: stir the whole and give it to the calf
todrink. At first itis necessary to make the calf drink, by presenting the finger
to it, but it soon learns to do so without this help, and will grow incomparably
fatter than by the old method.
The economical advantages resulting from it are as fullows:—According to the
old method, the calf intended for slaughter is made to suck for three weeks, and
those intended for agriculture, from six to eight weeks. Suppose the cow gives
| only a moderate quantity of milk, the value of it will amount, in three weeks, to
nearly the value ofthe calf. If, on the contrary, we rear a calf according to this
method, we constme during ihe three weeks only three quarts of oatmeal,

| To CLEAN TURKEY CARPETS.—TO revive the color of a Turkey carpet, beat it
| well with a stick tlii the dust is all got out; then, with a lemon or sorrel juice, |
| take out the spots of ink, if the carpet be stained with any; wash it in cold water, |
| and afterwards shake out all the water from the threads of the carpet. When it |
is thoroughly dry, rub it all over with the crumb of a hot wheaten loaf; and, if |
the weather is very fine, hang it out in the open air a night or two.
Excess of ceremony shows want of breeding. That civility is best which ex- |
cludes all superfluous formality.

Tre Use or Sutrnur In DEstROYING INSECTS ON PLANTS, AND ITS BENEFIT FOR |
VEGETATION.—Tie up some flower of sulphur ina piece of muslin or fine linen, |
and with this the leaves of young shoots of plants should be dusted; or it may be
thrown on them by means of a common swawn’s-down puff, or even by a dredging-
box.
Fresh assurances have repeatedly been received of the powerful influence of sul-
phur against the whole tribe of insects and worms which infest and prey on vege- |
tables. Sulphur has also been found to promote the health of plants, on which it |
was sprinkled; and that peach-trees, in particular, were remarkably improved by
it, and seemed to absorb it. It has likewise been observed, that the verdure, and
other healthful appeaiances, were perceptibly increased ; for the quantity of new |
shoots and leaves formed subsequently to the operation, and having no sulphur on |
their surface, served as a kind of comparative index, and pointed out distinctly
| the accumulation of health.

substance have been pared, so as to render the whole as smooth and even as pos-
sible. The varnish must be applied in dry weather, in order that it may attach
itself properly.

Tomato Savce.—Crush half a dozen, more or less, of very ripe, red tomatoes; |
pick out the seeds, and squeeze the water from them; put them into a stew-pan, |
| with two or three finely-sliced shulots, and a little gravy: simmer till nearly dry; |
| when add half a pint of brown sauce. and simmer twenty minutes longer; then |
rub it through a tammy into a clean stew-pan; season with Cayenne pepper and |
salt, a little glaze, and lemon juice; simmer a few minutes, and serve. Tarragon
or Chili vinegar are sometimes added; and sliced oniens may be substituted for |
the shalots.

Fatrentne Cuicxens.—Take, for that purpose, a quanity of rice, and grind or
pound it into a coarse flour; mix sufficient for present use with milk and a little

more, into the troughs belonging to their coops. It must be eaten while warm;

oatmeal and treacle, combined till it crumbles, is said to form a food for chickens,
of which they are so fond, and with which they thrive so rapidly, that at the end

192. Rivers.—The Elbe, a large German river, washes the
southern frontier of the kingdom; but from the flatness of the
surface, and the limited extent of the land-tracts, it is impos-
sible that Denmark should have any large river of its own.
The only one worthy of mention is the Eider, which separates
Schleswig from Holsiein.
198. Lakes.—There are about 400 lakes scattered over the
surface, but most of them are very small, The largest are
Ersom and Arre, in the north of Seeland.
Fiords and Gulfs—The Liimfiord extends from the Kattegst nearly
across the whole breadth of North Jiitland; at first in a narrow stream,
but afterwards expanding into a broad basin, interrupted by tongues,
and studded with small islands. - It is separated from the German Sea
only by a narrow strip of land, which was broken through by the waves.
in 1825; and the Agger Canal, of little commercial value, has since
been formed at the breach. Smaller fiords in the mainland are Rings-
kidbing, Nissum, and the bays of Kalée and Flensborg ; in Seeland,
the Ise-fiord ; and in Fiihnen, the Odensee-fiord.
194, Straits, Sounds, &c.—The Skagerrack, the Kattegat, the
Sound, the Great and Little Belts, all lead into the Baltic; and
the toll which the king of Denmark receives for the p e of
foreign vessels through them, forms an important item of his
revenue.
195. Climate.—The air is humid and cloudy; and the climate
much milder than its latitude would indicate.
196. Soil and Vegetation.—In Jiitland and the Duchies, the
soil is almost entirely alluvial, much of it being covered with a
vegetable mould well adapted for cultivation, while the marshy
districts produce excellent pasturage.
In the north-west parts of Jiitland, however, the higher grounds are
sandy, and for the most part covered with bent, heath, and brambles.
The <ul of the islands is of moderate fertility, and throughout thei«
2-3 frequent accumulations of peat. The forests are not now ex‘ 71". ¢,
and are chiefly confined to the eastern coasts of the peninsula sii t/:2
isjands of Seeland and Fihnen.
197. Animals.—In losing their vast forests, the Danish
territories have also lost the larger wild animals.
The wolf has entirely disappeared ; the wild-boar has become very
rare; the stag and fallow-deer remain only in parks; but the fox,
marten, polecat, and various smaller quadrupeds, exist in great num-
bers. Game is abundant; the shores and fiords abound in aquatic
birds; and the surrounding seas furnish unfailing supplies of white
and flat fish.
